ideas.idea: The management textbook itself moves planning and control towards the people doing the work as uncertainty increases.
ideas.note: The apparent contradiction is often with selective corporate practice.

ideas.idea: Specific, difficult goals can improve performance more than vague instructions to do one's best.
ideas.note: Includes the 94% log-loading example; examples are not separate ideas.

ideas.idea: Retain precise targets for stable, repeatable work rather than applying the critique to every task.
ideas.note: Goal planning suits the less uncertain technical core.

ideas.idea: Directional domain planning suits uncertain situations and senior levels better than prematurely precise goals.
ideas.note: Distinct from decentralising decision authority.

ideas.idea: The more complex a change, the more employees should help plan and implement it.
Kotter's top-down change model fits reasonably predictable changes, but excluding employees from shaping plans can generate resistance.
Management textbooks assume a generally predictable, linear and centrally controllable organisational world.
ideas.note: Mechanistic models are described, but the textbook also teaches uncertainty, emergence and decentralisation.

ideas.idea: Uncertainty, friction and disorder are inherent operating conditions that detailed central plans cannot eliminate.
Excessive central control and repeated upward approval slow decisions and suppress local initiative.
ideas.note: Corporate approval chains are applications of the doctrine's mechanism.

ideas.idea: Purpose can remain valid after changing conditions make rigid cascaded tasks or targets obsolete.
Attach a concise statement of purpose, such as an in-order-to clause, to each objective.
Delegate the method of execution and permit teams to adapt within senior intent without waiting for permission.
ideas.note: Includes mission tactics and authority to depart from obsolete plans.

ideas.idea: People should understand their commander's or manager's intent at least two levels above them.
ideas.note: The numerical depth is explicit in the source.

ideas.idea: Designate one main effort and give it priority for resources while accepting prudent risk elsewhere.
Longer planning horizons should carry less imposed precision because influence over distant events is weaker.
Information technology and live dashboards can tempt leaders into excessive direct control of subordinates.
ideas.note: The dashboard is an application of the information-technology warning.

ideas.idea: Use implicit communication rather than relying entirely on detailed explicit instructions.
Balanced scorecards dissipate attention across dozens of competing metrics, unlike the military's single main effort.
ideas.note: The textbook teaches multiple balanced perspectives, not necessarily dozens of competing priorities.

ideas.idea: Critical Path Method scheduling assumes task durations are known with certainty.
ideas.note: This is an explicit assumption of CPM, not of all planning methods.

ideas.idea: Pressure to meet a fixed date or production target can progressively consume safety or quality margins and accumulate hidden risk.
Visible production results crowd out preventive work unless leaders deliberately reinforce prevention behaviours.
For each KPI, identify and monitor the useful work people might stop doing in order to meet it.
ideas.note: Direct application of the warning about rewarded behaviours displacing more productive ones.

ideas.idea: Repeated successful outcomes can normalise known deviations and breed complacency without establishing that the underlying risk is acceptable.
Good results can come from questionable behaviour and poor results from reasonable behaviour, so outcomes alone misjudge performance.
Results metrics are lagging indicators and do not establish current organisational health or predict continued performance.
Choose indicators for their relevance to performance rather than simply because they are easy to count.
A barrage of statistics used to grade a unit obscures meaning and suppresses discussion in learning reviews.
Keep useful targets and data rather than concluding that measurement itself is the problem.
ideas.note: Aggressive schedules can be healthy; statistics can supply objective feedback.

ideas.idea: Quantitative evidence can help lower-status technical voices be heard when rank otherwise determines credibility.
ideas.note: CAIB also warns that demanding numbers from those voices can inhibit them.

ideas.idea: Separate technical, quality or safety authority from managers responsible for cost and schedule, with independent resources and real authority.
Rigid hierarchy and proper-channel requirements can block technical warnings and substitute procedural authority for expertise.
During complex operational problems or crises, defer decisions to relevant expertise rather than rank.
Requiring concerned engineers to prove danger before management responds reverses the appropriate burden of proof for high-risk operations.
For high-consequence work, require evidence of safety and pause or stop when safety remains uncertain.
ideas.note: Includes stop-work authority and the prove-no-harm question.

ideas.idea: Senior leaders should actively seek dissent, challenge unanimity and amplify weak warning signals.
Information becomes abbreviated and simplified as it moves up a hierarchy, allowing weak signals to disappear before a steering committee sees them.
Consensus sign-offs can diffuse ownership so that everyone signs but no one is effectively accountable.
Give each steering decision one explicitly named owner.
ideas.note: The sources criticise dispersed accountability and require named action responsibility.

ideas.idea: A steering committee should test green reports and hunt for bad news rather than merely collect reassuring status and signatures.
Leaders create the culture and remain responsible for the systemic effects of their own targets, schedules and decisions.
Include senior leaders' and the commissioning committee's own decisions in incident or change reviews.
Use someone outside the steering committee to review the committee's decisions.
ideas.note: Independent assessment plus scrutiny of commissioning leaders supports this application.

ideas.idea: A senior human-performance steering committee can be useful when it monitors trends, assessments and corrective actions and holds managers accountable.
High-reliability practice rejects central oversight and steering committees in favour of decentralised frontline authority.
ideas.note: Decentralisation is real, but DOE committees and CAIB independent central authority contradict the blanket claim.

ideas.idea: Individual performance scores can attribute to personal merit or effort results that were substantially shaped by organisational conditions.
Human errors are often symptoms of latent organisational weaknesses and error-provoking job conditions rather than sufficient explanations of failure.
Human fallibility is normal, including among capable and motivated people, rather than simply a sign of deficient personal motivation.
At least 85% of facility-event causes originate in organisational processes and culture.
ideas.note: An estimate in the handbook, not a universal company statistic.

ideas.idea: Perhaps 90% or more of unsafe acts fall into the blameless category.
Latent organisational weaknesses cause 81% of operational failures, while active worker errors account for 19%.
ideas.note: The 81/19 split concerns 270 errors in 35 nuclear events, not percentages of failures generally.

ideas.idea: Over 90% of operational errors are organisationally induced.
ideas.note: The handbook estimates blameless unsafe acts at 90% and organisational origins of event causes at 85%; neither is this claim.

ideas.idea: Retraining people for an automatic, unintended slip is ineffective because they already know the task.
Punishment or blame for reported mistakes discourages disclosure of errors, near misses and workarounds, leaving leaders blind to risks.
Protect learning reviews from pay, appraisal and disciplinary processes through an explicit, preferably written firewall.
ideas.note: The signed protection for learning information supports the appraisal application.

ideas.idea: Use the substitution test to ask whether similarly qualified peers would have acted the same way in the same circumstances before blaming an individual.
Distinguish honest error from reckless or knowing misconduct rather than treating blamelessness as absence of all individual consequences.
Forward-looking accountability means giving an honest account and improving the system, rather than simply assigning punishment.
Use candid, participatory after-action reviews in which people of different ranks contribute rather than relying on one-way managerial critiques.
An after-action review does not grade success or failure; it identifies strengths to sustain and weaknesses to improve.
Structure learning discussions around intended performance, what actually happened, why it happened and how to improve.
Hold after-action learning discussions during or immediately after important events while experience is fresh.
Evaluate decisions in the context of what participants knew and intended at the time rather than judging them through hindsight and outcomes.
Forced ranking can foster internal competition and undermine collaboration, a problem already acknowledged in the management textbook.
The textbook reports substantial executive doubt that conventional performance management improves engagement or performance.
ideas.note: The reported survey figure is 58%.

ideas.idea: The textbook recommends performance-contingent rewards as a source of motivation.
ideas.note: F contrasts this with outcome-based judgement; the distinction is recorded separately.

ideas.idea: The textbook endorses a nine-box performance-versus-potential grid for talent assessment.
The textbook itself warns that excessive controls and inappropriate goals can produce dysfunctional behaviour.
Outcome-based appraisal can punish a bold unsuccessful attempt while rewarding safe inaction.
ideas.note: Direct synthesis of outcome bias and the military treatment of boldness and inaction.

ideas.idea: Do not make learning depend on serious harm: a near miss can reveal the same conditions as a fatal accident.
Compare work as managers imagine it with work as people actually perform it to expose systemic vulnerabilities.
ideas.note: J explicitly recommends reviews to uncover this gap.

ideas.idea: Learning reviews and just-culture frameworks must be entirely divorced from management oversight committees because governance destroys psychological safety.
ideas.note: The sources protect learning information from discipline; LFUO also provides a Learning Review Board and NHS retains HR involvement.

ideas.idea: Repurpose steering committees solely to fund and fix system traps surfaced by frontline learning reviews.
ideas.note: Funding improvements is consistent; the restriction to this sole function is not supported.

ideas.idea: Blameless reviews ensure that operational reality reaches senior leaders instantly.
ideas.note: The sources support improved disclosure and prompt reviews, not guaranteed instantaneous visibility.

ideas.idea: Marine doctrine treats overbold mistakes leniently while dealing severely with inaction or timidity.
Military action under uncertainty conflicts with the nuclear and spaceflight default of proving safety before proceeding.
ideas.note: A difference of operating emphasis, not proof that either tradition always forbids the other stance.

ideas.idea: Choose faster initiative for reversible or competitive experiments and stricter checks for irreversible or high-consequence decisions.
ideas.note: The sources differentiate urgency and irreversible harm, but do not make reversibility a sufficient rule for selecting an entire doctrine.

ideas.idea: Military doctrine does not require rushed decisions when time is not a limiting factor, such as deliberate planning.
High reliability requires the ability to centralise or decentralise according to the situation.
Nuclear safety's overriding safe-work priority differs from the Forest Service's mission-first acceptance of inherent hazard.
ideas.note: B states the Forest Service half without contrasting the nuclear definition.

ideas.idea: The Marine duty to act, with sanctions for timidity, differs from just-culture frameworks that shield many unintended system-induced errors.
ideas.note: A difference in emphasis; neither source exempts all misconduct.

ideas.idea: The traditions draw different boundaries for blame: NHS and DOE use decision tests, Forest Service protects learning and excludes reckless harm, and military doctrine tolerates honest boldness but censures recklessness or evasion.
Columbia's investigation protected witness statements while leaving personal accountability to a separate investigation.
Forest Service facilitated learning analysis provides absolute immunity from discipline, unlike DOE and NHS culpability processes.
ideas.note: Review information has strong protection, but external legal action and separately investigated reckless misconduct are not immunised.

ideas.idea: Army AARs evaluate against task standards, whereas wildfire learning reviews emphasise why actions made sense in their original context.
Army reviews lead to prompt retraining of deficient tasks and revision of standing procedures.
The Army's corrective retraining and action plans contrast with wildfire reviews' protection against forced retraining and reluctance to impose fixes.
ideas.note: The disagreement concerns how learning leads to imposed corrective action.

ideas.idea: DOE preserves root-cause analysis but directs it towards preventable organisational weaknesses rather than stopping at the person who erred.
Inattention and failure to follow a procedure are not adequate root causes because they do not explain the underlying conditions.
Forest Service facilitated learning analyses reject causal statements and single root-cause fixes for complex events, unlike DOE causal analysis and Columbia's structural prescriptions.
Complex accidents arise from dynamic networks of interacting conditions rather than one isolatable root cause.
Recommendations, extra rules and reorganisations can add complexity and create new ways to fail.
Jumping straight to an action list can displace learning and create an unwarranted belief that the problem has been solved.
Develop and vet new rules or recommendations with the people who will do the work before adopting them.
Audit previous corrective actions for how many added process steps and how many removed them.
ideas.note: A reasonable proposed measurement of complexity; no source located prescribes this add-versus-remove count.

ideas.idea: Use root-cause analysis for process or equipment failures and contextual reconstruction for pressured judgement calls.
ideas.note: The simple/complicated versus complex distinction supplies the general basis.

ideas.idea: Use a single incident primarily for contextual learning, but treat a pattern as grounds for structural change.
ideas.note: Single-data-point caution and structural reform are supported; this incident-versus-pattern decision threshold is added.

ideas.idea: Reorganisation initially raises error risk because old and new practices compete and institutional memory can be lost.
Post-accident reforms can erode over time, so issuing a reform is not evidence it will remain effective.
Replacing or removing individuals cannot by itself solve systemic organisational problems.
Formal procedure adherence and checking in nuclear operations contrast with military freedom to improvise and depart from obsolete plans.
DOE's procedure-adherence model contrasts with wildfire recognition that routine practical adaptations and shortcuts are part of real work.
ideas.note: DOE also acknowledges inappropriate procedures; this is a difference in operational response.

ideas.idea: Nuclear HPI aims at complete elimination of human error.
ideas.note: DOE explicitly recognises human fallibility; zero significant events is different from eliminating all human error.

ideas.idea: Use deliberate self-checking to reduce operational errors.
Military unified line command and decentralised initiative differ from Columbia's independent central technical authority and checks on programme managers.
ideas.note: Both retain authority, but allocate technical and operational decisions differently.

ideas.idea: Combine local autonomy for ordinary execution with separate independent authority over core quality and risk standards.
ideas.note: A direct application of the distinct execution and technical-standards responsibilities.

ideas.idea: Feedback loops, time delays and accumulations make organisational interventions behave differently from a linear X-causes-Y model.
A short-term intervention can provoke delayed compensating responses that worsen the problem it was meant to solve.
ideas.note: The sources carry the policy-resistance mechanism even without that exact label.

ideas.idea: Aggressive cost cuts or compressed schedules can increase rework, burnout and later bottlenecks, eroding capacity or increasing total cost.
ideas.note: Workload/burnout feedback and schedule-induced risk are supported; the combined cost-cutting, rework and total-cost chain is more specific.

ideas.idea: Cutting support staff to improve short-term margins exemplifies the shifting-the-burden archetype.
ideas.note: The archetype requires a symptomatic fix that weakens a fundamental solution; that structure is not established by the answer's example.

ideas.idea: Map feedback loops, stocks and delays before structural interventions to anticipate unintended consequences.
Military reliance on experienced tactical intuition contrasts with systems thinking's warning that intuition misreads feedback, delays and accumulations.
ideas.note: MCDP itself also allows more analytical decisions at higher levels.

ideas.idea: Use experienced intuition at the operational edge and deliberate systems mapping for executive decisions about incentives and structure.
ideas.note: The sources explicitly distinguish tactical and senior analysis and offer mapping to challenge intuition.

ideas.idea: A roughly 300-person company occupies a distinctive size threshold between informal coordination and bureaucracy.
ideas.note: Growth and formalisation are discussed; no general 300-person threshold was found.

ideas.idea: As executives become removed from frontline work, formal reports can conceal the gap between managerial assumptions and operating reality.
ideas.note: Application to a 300-person firm does not require a numerical size threshold.

ideas.idea: Functional resource pools and narrow specialisation create dependencies and handoffs that slow end-to-end delivery.
Create complete cross-functional units with broad mandates to deliver customer value with fewer external handoffs.
Narrow output metrics and capability-specific goals encourage local optimisation rather than shared customer or whole-business outcomes.
ideas.note: K carries the local-optimisation critique as well as the team-design recommendation.

ideas.idea: Standard textbooks prescribe maximising every functional department's resource utilisation to 100%.
ideas.note: The primer describes this Resource Topology; no textbook prescription to maximise every department to 100% was found.

ideas.idea: Scrum uses self-managing cross-functional teams without internal subteams or hierarchies.
ideas.note: Open Kanban does not require eliminating existing roles or titles.

ideas.idea: Scrum and Org Topologies reject specialised parallel technical oversight altogether, conflicting with Columbia's independent technical authority.
ideas.note: No source bans external technical oversight; Scrum's no-hierarchy rule is internal to the Scrum Team.

ideas.idea: Scrum uses fixed iterations, commonly described as one to four weeks, to create a cadence for empirical inspection and adaptation.
ideas.note: The field guide states 1–4 weeks; the 2020 Scrum Guide says one month or less.

ideas.idea: The Sprint Backlog is a delivery commitment in Scrum.
ideas.note: Scrum commits to the Sprint Goal; the Sprint Backlog is updated and its scope can be renegotiated.

ideas.idea: Open Kanban and system dynamics oppose fixed iterations because timeboxes create artificial batching and scheduling overhead.
ideas.note: Open Kanban supports smaller batches but does not state this anti-timebox argument; no matching systems-dynamics passage was found.

ideas.idea: Continuous flow can release work as it becomes ready rather than holding it for a batch or iteration boundary.
ideas.note: The broader Kanban library passage supports this, although Open Kanban does not explicitly oppose Sprints.

ideas.idea: Limit work in progress, including active executive initiatives, to improve flow and reduce cycle time.
ideas.note: Applying the general WIP principle to executive initiatives is supported.

ideas.idea: Reduce batch sizes to accelerate completion and feedback.
Little's Law gives cycle time as throughput divided by work in progress.
ideas.note: The answer displays the ratio inverted; open-practice-library.md:21162 gives Cycle Time = WIP / Throughput.

ideas.idea: Most work in a commercial quarter is reversible, so conventional targets and reviews are generally tolerable there.
ideas.note: The prevalence of reversible commercial work and the resulting tolerability claim are not established by the sources.

ideas.idea: Wildfire reluctance to issue recommendations may be impractical when a business needs a decision by Friday.
ideas.note: A reasonable concern about transferring the approach; the library does not establish this business-deadline trade-off.

ideas.idea: Evidence connecting formal planning with better financial returns is limited even in the textbook's own account.
Review achievement of the underlying purpose rather than scoring only whether a target number was hit.
ideas.note: Purpose is predominant when task and intent diverge.

ideas.idea: When speed matters, act on incomplete information rather than waiting for certainty or a perfect plan.
ideas.note: Distinct from the diagnosis that central approval slows execution.

ideas.idea: Judge a change programme by whether bad news reaches its steering committee faster.
ideas.note: The sources urge stronger warning signals but do not prescribe information-travel time as the programme's evaluation measure.

ideas.idea: Penalising individual errors causes organisations to normalise operational deviations.
ideas.note: Blame suppresses learning and past success normalises deviations; this specific causal connection between the two is not established.

ideas.idea: Confidence that an organisation already has a strong safety culture can itself conceal systemic weaknesses.
Subordinates should offer honest disagreement before a decision and support the decision once it is made.
After apparent success, ask what nearly went wrong or what deviation the team got away with.
ideas.note: Self-analysis after success and the warning against success-based complacency support this application.

ideas.idea: Nuclear work uses deliberate pre-job planning and hazard analysis rather than relying entirely on rapid improvisation.
Punishment has adverse effects and should not be the main motivational tool, a reservation already present in the textbook.
ideas.note: The textbook advises pairing punishment with reinforcement and describes its negative side effects.

ideas.idea: Army corrective retraining contrasts with DOE's view that retraining automatic slips is ineffective.
ideas.note: The traditions address different kinds of performance problem.

ideas.idea: Peer checks provide another person's scrutiny to prevent mistakes during critical work.
Three-way repeat-back communication reduces misunderstandings during safety-critical work.
Layer multiple defences so that one human error does not directly produce a harmful event.
Nuclear doctrine treats every unapproved departure from a written procedure as unacceptable or error-provoking.
ideas.note: DOE requires adherence to workable procedures but recognises flawed procedures and necessary system-induced violations.

ideas.idea: Incident reviews can focus almost entirely on people at the scene while failing to examine decisions by commissioning officials and senior supervisors.
ideas.note: Distinct from the recommendation to include those leaders in future reviews.

ideas.idea: DOE targets zero significant events through error reduction and defences, whereas Marine doctrine explicitly rejects a zero-defects mentality.
ideas.note: Zero significant events does not mean that people become incapable of error.
